## Paper 2 · Session 04 · What happens next to a social group {.center .scrollable}

## The data, and the models {.scrollable}

**Saganowski et al. (2019)** · one row = one group of students messaging each other at UC Irvine,
in one week (498 groups). Outcome: what happened next — **dissolving** 35.5%, **shrinking** 25.9%,
**growing** 25.1%, **continuing** 10.0%. Features: `log2_size` (+1 = twice as big),
`avg_degree`, `aging`.

| Steps | Model | Session-04 tabs, copied line for line |
|---|---|---|
| 3–5 | **binary**: does it dissolve? | LR 6 · LR 7 · LR 8 |
| 6–8 | **ordinal**: shrinking < continuing < growing | OLR 3 · OLR 4 · OLR 5 |
| 9–11 | **multinomial**: four events vs dissolving | MLR 3 · MLR 4 · MLR 5 |

::: {.muted}
Only the data and the variable names change.
:::

{{< include _solutions-r3.qmd >}}

## What you should find {.scrollable}

| Model | Size effect | In probabilities |
|---|---|---|
| binary | odds ratio **0.565** per doubling | P(dissolve): 0.41 at 4 members, 0.18 at 16 |
| ordinal | odds ratio **0.262** per doubling | P(shrink): 0.26 at 4 members, 0.84 at 16 |
| multinomial | RRR **3.22**, shrinking vs dissolving | 4 → 32 members: P(dissolve) 0.42 → 0.08, P(shrink) 0.14 → 0.87 |

::: {.check}
Large groups rarely vanish in one week — but they lose members. Three models, three questions,
one story.
:::

## What it does not license {.scrollable}

::: {.tight}
- **No causal reading.** Adding members would not by itself keep a group alive.
- **No claim beyond these groups.** One university, one tracking method, weekly windows.
- **Nothing on splitting or merging.** At 3.4% together, they are too rare to model here.
:::
